title: Argentina’s central bank asks how disinflation could translate into lasting investment
bank: Banco Central de la República Argentina
summary: At Argentina’s 2026 Monetary and Banking Conference, BCRA President Santiago Bausili posed a question that an inflation reading alone cannot settle. Once greater price stability has been achieved, what would turn it into sustained growth and higher living standards? The central bank’s 19 November account of the conference records several answers worth distinguishing. Its president emphasized productivity and opportunity. Its vice president focused on the institutions that support monetary credibility. Invited researchers and central bankers discussed investment, innovation, fiscal rules and exchange-rate arrangements. The release reports their subjects and selected remarks. It supplies neither a common conclusion from the speakers nor a decision to adopt any of the arrangements discussed (opening and closing sections).

President Javier Milei’s closing remarks set out the administration’s assessment of stabilization. He cited annual retail price growth of around 30% and a latest monthly wholesale price rise of 1.6%, and described the disinflation programme as successful. The release also records his discussion of fiscal balance and the condition of the central bank’s balance sheet. The retail and wholesale figures refer to different prices over different intervals. Comparing their numerical levels would say little about the speed of current disinflation. Nor does the release contain a price time series, a decomposition of the moderation or an estimate of how much each part of the programme contributed. The claim of success is explicitly Milei’s assessment (paragraphs on the closing address).

The conference linked monetary stability to the allocation of resources through several distinct mechanisms. Philippe Aghion discussed innovation, reallocation and barriers to entry. Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras and former Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Ian Macfarlane explored how stable money can influence private investment and resource allocation. A session on Chile and Norway examined structural fiscal rules, sovereign savings funds and the variability of economic cycles. Together these contributions frame a question for Argentina about whether predictability allows firms to invest or enter a market. The account gives no measured effect for Argentina from these international examples, and lists the savings funds and fiscal rules as topics of the comparative session (sections on the programme and international experiences).

The release also identifies two different ways to investigate monetary credibility. Fernando Alvarez presented a model of widening exchange-rate bands based on Argentina’s exchange-rate framework. BCRA Vice President Vladimir Werning spoke about the central bank charter, recapitalization, the return of domestic savings held abroad and disinflation. A theoretical model of how bands operate addresses a different question from an assessment of the central bank’s balance sheet or legal authority. The article gives no calibrated band parameters, timetable for a charter reform or estimate of future inflows of savings. Other sessions covered market expectations, financial innovation, stablecoins, tokenization and artificial intelligence. They establish how broad the conference agenda was without supplying quantified effects on money demand. The distinction matters for readers looking for actionable policy information in an event held on 16–17 November in Buenos Aires. The full talks are linked from the central bank’s conference resources, while the November 19 release records the questions and speakers.

questions.question: Which balance-sheet and legal changes underpin the vice president’s assessment of monetary credibility?
questions.detail: The release names recapitalization and reform of the central bank charter alongside disinflation and returning savings. It does not set out implementation dates, the size of capital changes or a measure of credibility. Consult the presentation, published charter documents and dated balance sheets to distinguish completed actions from proposals, then compare them with changes in the maturity and currency composition of private saving.

questions.question: What mechanism does the widening-band model imply for exchange-rate expectations?
questions.detail: The account identifies the model’s author and connection with Argentina’s framework but gives no equations, calibration or conclusions. The presentation is needed to establish how the boundaries move, what intervention is assumed and whether market participants anticipate changes. Compare the model’s implications with observed exchange-rate and expectation data only after specifying which period and operating rules the exercise is meant to describe.

questions.question: What evidence would connect disinflation to a lasting increase in productive investment?
questions.detail: Several speakers discuss stability, reallocation and entry, but none of the evidence for a causal link is reproduced in the release. Seek sector-level investment, firm entry and productivity data around the stabilization period. Comparing firms exposed to different financing conditions, alongside the original international presentations, could help distinguish gains following a more predictable monetary environment from the ordinary recovery of demand.

limitation: The official release summarizes selected conference remarks. It provides no transcripts, research exhibits or estimates from the individual presentations.
